site: Sigiriya (Sīgiriya, Sinhagiri, "Lion Rock"), Matale District, Sri Lanka. The Lion Gate: the lion-staircase terrace on a plateau about halfway up the north side of the rock, c. AD 477–495 (Kassapa I). 7.957 N, 80.757 E (Pleiades 50266), which matches the atlas entry (7.96, 80.76). Asset id map-monument-ch07-monsoon.
view: Stand on the lion terrace near its northern edge, on the line of the stair, at a person's eye height. Look south, up the line of the stair (the paws face north: Bell describes them on 'the north façade'), and tilt up. LOWER THIRD: the terrace floor, reddish earth with brick edging, running into the picture. The two paws sit left and right of centre with their claws toward the viewer, and a flight of steps climbs between them to the foot of the cliff. UPPER TWO THIRDS: the sheer north cliff of the rock rising to the summit edge. Let the rock narrow slightly toward the top, as it does when a camera tilts up, so a wedge of brochure sky shows in each upper corner, and keep the summit line flat. Put a fringe of dry-zone tree canopy at the lower left and right edges, where the terrace drops away. CROPPED OUT: the west face (off to the right), which carries the mirror-wall gallery and the fresco pocket. The water gardens at the western foot and Pidurangala rock, about 1.5 to 2 km north, are behind the viewer. Every modern fitting is left out. WHY THIS VIEW: the rock takes its name from the lion, "of which only the paws remain" (UNESCO Courier 1988), so a brochure headline leans on the paws. This is the only view that holds both halves of the name, the lion and the rock. The other classic view, the whole rock from the west over the water gardens, shrinks at 92 × 70 to a featureless flat-topped block that could be any mesa, and it hides the lion. The existing code silhouette mixes the two viewpoints: the whole rock outline with the terrace at plain level. The painting replaces it with this one real viewpoint.

elements.fact: Only the forepaws of the lion survive. Everything that stood above them is gone. They are built masonry, brick with lime plaster, not carved from the living rock. H.C.P. Bell (Archaeological Survey of Ceylon) uncovered them in 1898 while following 'the curved ground line of the north façade to the massive brick structure', and described 'the huge claws – even to the dewclaw – of a once gigantic lion, conventionalized in brick and plaster' (Bell, quoted in secondary sources; the report itself was not reached). UNESCO's brief description has 'a gigantic lion constructed of bricks and plaster' (confirmed in a search snippet of whc.unesco.org/en/list/202). The paws are the front of a brick mass along a curved line, not two free-standing sculptures on an open floor. One tour source calls them 'stone lion paws' and another says 'carved from the natural rock': both are wrong.

The claws point north, toward the viewer, and project forward from the brickwork in high relief. Bell first took them for 'very roughly moulded elephant heads – three on either side of the central staircase – projecting from the brick work in high relief, life size'. So each paw shows three large claws, and the two paws mirror each other; the existing silhouette also has three. Bell adds that the dewclaw is modelled too. Where the dewclaw sits, and whether a fourth small toe shows from the front, is not settled (see contested). Still count and place them on a photograph before painting.

Each claw is about the size of a life-size elephant's head (Bell's first reading of them, above). Travel sources give each paw as at least 10 feet (about 3 m) tall and 10 feet wide, which fits Bell's scale. So each paw stands higher than a person on the steps between them. The 3 m figure is from a weak source: treat it as a proportion, not a measurement.

The final ascent began with a stair between the paws, which led on (by reconstruction) into the lion's mouth and, in Bell's words, 'through whose body passed the winding stairway, connecting the upper and lower galleries'. The paws and the first steps survive. The steps are stone (one source says limestone), human-scale, and rise away from the viewer toward the cliff.

A plateau on the northern side of the rock, about halfway up (Wikipedia; also secondary summaries of the Culavamsa), at the foot of the sheer upper cliff. It is not at the level of the surrounding plain. The ground is dry-zone reddish earth and gravel, edged with brick. The earth and edging are a judgement, not checked against a photograph.

A sheer, bare, near-vertical rock face: UNESCO calls it a 180 m 'granite peak' and the UNESCO Courier 'an immense rock of red gneiss, 180 m high'. It is not a vegetated hill, not a dome and not a cone. Its colour, a weathered warm reddish grey with dark vertical streaks, is a judgement from 'red gneiss' and remembered photographs; no source checked it in this research.
Broadly flat. Kassapa's palace survives on it only as foundations and rock-cut cisterns. From the terrace nothing stands on the skyline.

Both are on the WEST face and are not visible from this viewpoint. The frescoes sit in a sheltered pocket 'halfway up the west face' (UNESCO Courier). The mirror wall is the polished plaster wall of the gallery that runs along the west face to the lion terrace. Neither appears on the cliff above the paws.

elements.element: Modern iron stairways, railings, the hornet shelter cage, signs, visitors
elements.fact: Metal stairs climb the rock above the paws to the summit ('the paws and first steps remain, followed by metal stairs leading toward the summit'). They are modern intrusions and are left out of the painting (see deliberatelyWrong).
Dry-zone forest canopy below and around the rock. Only a fringe of treetops shows at the lower edges, beyond the terrace.

mustBeRight: Exactly two paws, one each side of a central flight of steps.
No lion head, mane, body or open jaws above the paws: the rest of the lion is gone.
The paws are masonry (brick-red with patches of pale plaster), clearly a different material and colour from the rock behind them.
The claws point toward the viewer and stand forward of the brickwork at terrace level.
Three large claws on each paw (Bell: 'three on either side of the central staircase'), and the two paws are mirror images of each other, same size and same count.
Each paw stands taller than a person on the steps would; each claw is roughly the size of an elephant's head.
The steps rise between the paws, away from the viewer, toward the cliff.
The rock behind is a sheer, near-vertical bare cliff, not a green hill, dome or cone.
The summit line is broadly flat with no building, wall, tower or roof on it.
No paintings of women on the cliff face in this view.
No gleaming mirror wall on the cliff face above the paws.
No water, moat or fountains in frame.
No stupa, Buddha image or temple anywhere in frame.
Nothing modern in frame: no iron stairways, handrails, cage, signs or visitors.
The rock and the paws are lit from the upper right.
deliberatelyWrong: The modern metal stairways on the rock above the paws, the handrails and the hornet shelter are left out. At 92 × 70 a zigzag of one-pixel rails reads as cracks or a scribble, and a brochure sells the fifth century, not the fittings.
The terrace is empty. It is never empty in life, but the brochure clears it, and figures at this size would be specks that confuse the reading of the paws' scale.

The light comes from the upper right, the set's convention (_brush.js B.LIGHT). Facing south, that is afternoon sun from the west. The sun stands north of due west in the afternoon only between the March and September equinoxes, and north of the zenith at noon only from about mid-April to late August (the site is at 8 degrees N). The north face is lit like this only in that half of the year, and the brochure picked that season.
The brochure sky: cleaner and bluer than a real dry-zone sky (the set's shared skyTop and skyLow).
The depth of the terrace is compressed and the cliff shortened, so the paws and the summit edge fit one 92 × 70 frame. Looking up from the terrace, the true cliff would fill far more of the view.
The bee and hornet colonies hanging on the rock face, the grooves cut for the original stair, and the lichen and weathering detail are left off: at this size they read as holes or damage.

The dewclaw Bell recorded on each paw is left off. At 92 x 70 it would be one or two pixels, and it would read as a fourth claw or as damage, breaking the three-claw reading. Its position was not verified in this research either.
The rock's colour is a brochure judgement: weathered warm reddish grey with dark vertical streaks, neither pale grey granite nor sunset orange. It was not matched to a photograph.

lighting: Bright afternoon sun from the upper right, the set's B.LIGHT. Facing south, that is sun from the west and a little north of it, raking across the north cliff and the fronts of the paws. The right-hand (west) flanks of the paws and of the steps catch the light. Their left sides and the claw undersides fall into the set's cool shadow mix. The cliff face is lit obliquely, so its dark streaks and overhangs model it. There is no cast shadow on the terrace floor beyond what the paws throw a little to the left. A brochure sky with no clouds over the summit.
pitfalls: Painting the paws as grey stone, or as carved out of the cliff. They are brick and plaster, the front of a brick structure standing on the terrace. Some tour text says 'stone paws': ignore it.
Completing the lion: a head, mane, jaws or body over the stair. Only the paws survive, and the rest is a reconstruction.

Giving the paws a housecat's four or five rounded toes, different claw counts left and right, or claws turned upward. Bell's report gives three large claws each side of the stair; paint three per paw.
Putting the famous painted women (the 'Sigiriya maidens') or the mirror wall on the face above the paws. Both are on the west face, out of this view.
Crowning the rock with a standing palace. The summit holds foundations and cisterns only.
Painting the rock as a smooth dome or a volcanic cone because of the popular 'magma plug' story. It is a sheer-sided, flat-topped block.
Grey granite colour, or the saturated orange of sunset photographs, instead of weathered reddish grey with dark streaks.
Adding the moat, water gardens or fountains in the foreground. They lie at the western foot of the rock, far below and behind this viewpoint.

Putting Pidurangala rock, its temple, a reclining Buddha or a stupa in the background. Pidurangala is about 1.5 to 2 km north, behind the viewer, and its cave temple (Pidurangala Raja Maha Viharaya) is an active place of worship with a large brick reclining Buddha (gate 6).
Using a Chinese guardian lion or the sword-bearing lion of the Sri Lankan flag as the model for the paws.
Painting the terrace at the level of the plain, as the current code silhouette does. From this viewpoint the terrace is the ground, and the cliff rises from its back edge.
Painting the modern iron stairway because every photograph shows it. It is deliberately left out.
Giving the paws the reptile, Ravana or bird (Gurula) reading from online videos. Those are fringe claims; the paws are a lion's, as the name Sihagiri says.
gate6: clear. Sigiriya is an archaeological site (UNESCO World Heritage 1982) and is not a place of active worship. The Buddhist monastery that followed Kassapa lasted to about the 13th–14th century and survives as ruins. Kassapa's parricide is a 5th-century chronicle story, not recent death or atrocity. It has no entry in arc.md section 4, and arc.md marks it 'Gate 6 clear'. That is why it can replace Angkor Wat (active temple, open ruling) without a designer ruling. One caution for the frame: Pidurangala, the neighbouring rock about 1.5 to 2 km north, has a working Buddhist cave temple (Pidurangala Raja Maha Viharaya) with a brick reclining Buddha about 12.5 m long, which travel sources say faces the lion's paws. It lies behind the viewer in this view and must stay out of frame, as must any stupa or Buddha image.
contested: Geology of the rock: 'a hardened magma plug from an extinct volcano' (Wikipedia and most tourist text) versus 'granite peak' (UNESCO WHC brief description) versus 'red gneiss' (UNESCO Courier, August 1988). A geoarchaeological study (ResearchGate, 'Utility of Inselbergs and Boulders as Rock-Shelter Monasteries') treats it as an inselberg; one geology summary gives a capstone of quartzo-feldspathic gneiss over hornblende-biotite gneiss, another says syenite. Sri Lanka's Grade 9 geography textbook lists Sigiriya among 'residual hills'. The painting needs none of these: a sheer, weathered reddish rock satisfies all of them.
Height: about 180 m (UNESCO WHC; UNESCO Courier 1988) versus 'nearly 200 m' (Wikipedia, tourism sources). The figure depends on where the plain is measured from.

What the lion looked like: 'the forequarters of a crouching lion' with 'galleries and staircases emerging from the mouth' (UNESCO) is a reconstruction from the surviving paws, the name Sihagiri and the Culavamsa (chapter 39: a staircase 'in the form of a lion'). No head or jaws survive. Popular text gives a brightly coloured lion about 35 m tall; no source for the figure was found. Fringe claims read the three-claw paws as a mythical bird's (Gurula), a reptile's or Ravana's feet. They have no scholarly support: exclude them and never state them.

Surviving frescoes: 21 figures (UNESCO Courier 1988) versus 22 (other sources). The graffiti refer to about 500 ladies, and Wikipedia says the paintings once covered much of the west face, 140 m by 40 m. Their identity (apsaras, court ladies, Paranavitana's cloud and lightning maidens) is unresolved.
Mirror-wall graffiti: Paranavitana (Sigiri Graffiti, 1956) published 685 verses of the 8th–10th centuries. Other counts are higher, with date ranges from the 6th to the 14th century.
Kassapa I's reign: 477–495 (UNESCO; Pleiades; arc.md). Other Sri Lankan chronologies shift it by a few years.

Claws and dewclaw: Bell saw three large claw projections each side of the stair and says the dewclaw is modelled too. Secondary sources then disagree: one describes three large toes and one small rudimentary toe per paw (a fringe video write-up, used only for the count), another says five toes and five claws including the dewclaw. Where the dewclaw sits (on a real lion it is on the inner side of the foreleg, higher up) and how much of it survives were not verified.
Size of the paws: 'at least 10 feet tall and 10 feet wide' (travel sources) fits Bell's 'life size' elephant-head claws, but no measured drawing was reached.
Pidurangala's distance: 'a little under two kilometres' to 'about 2.4 km' north (travel guides, probably by path). The earlier '1 km' was wrong or too short.

repoCorrections: content/map/README.md, vignettes table, row 7 still reads 'Angkor Wat | Five towers in a quincunx...'. src/map/atlas.ts and src/map/monuments.ts switched chapter 7 to Sigiriya ('lion-paws') in commit 856cda3, but the table was not updated. The row should name Sigiriya and give what must be right about the outline: two brick-and-plaster forepaws, claws toward the viewer, the steps between them, the sheer rock above with a flat summit line and no buildings, nothing else of the lion.

src/map/monuments.ts, the 'lion-paws' comment says 'a plug of old magma'. That is stated as fact but is contested: UNESCO says granite, the UNESCO Courier 1988 says red gneiss, and Sri Lanka's geography textbook calls Sigiriya a residual hill. Reword neutrally ('a sheer rock standing out of the plain').

content/research/arc.md, chapter 7 table: the 'Rock plug' wording for Sigiriya has the same problem. Per content/research/README.md the research is corrected first, to neutral wording such as 'sheer rock'.

content/research/arc.md, section 6 (Imagery risk), chapter 7 row: 'Archaeological Survey of India reports for Chand Baori and Sigiriya' is wrong for Sigiriya, which is in Sri Lanka. Its reports are the Archaeological Survey of Ceylon's (H.C.P. Bell's Annual Reports, from the 1890s), then Sri Lanka's Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund (Cultural Triangle project, 1980s). The ASI reference is right for Chand Baori only.

src/map/monuments.ts, the 'lion-paws' silhouette puts the terrace at the level of the plain, at the foot of the whole rock outline. The lion terrace is actually on a platform at the foot of the sheer upper cliff, about halfway up the rock. That is acceptable only as a listed brochure compression; the painted view from the terrace replaces it.

src/map/monuments.ts, the 'lion-paws' comment says 'the rest of the lion, head and body, is gone'. It is safer to say 'whatever stood above the paws is gone', because the head and jaws are a reconstruction, not a recorded find.
confidence: Medium. Web verification this session was limited to search snippets: WebSearch worked (11 of the 12 allowed searches used), but WebFetch was blocked for every page tried (archaeology.lk, lakpura.com, overatours.com, amahvanniarachchy.wordpress.com, heritagelk.weebly.com), as for whc.unesco.org, Wikipedia and archive.org before. Now verified, in snippets: UNESCO's 'gigantic lion constructed of bricks and plaster'; Bell's own 1898 description (as quoted by archaeology.lk and others), which gives the north façade, brick and plaster, three claws on each side of the central stair, a modelled dewclaw and claws of 'life size' elephant-head scale; the terrace halfway up the north side; stone steps between the paws; Culavamsa chapter 39's lion staircase (secondary); Pidurangala's active temple and reclining Buddha, and its distance corrected from about 1 km to about 1.5 to 2 km. Earlier verified, and unchanged: the UNESCO Courier 1988 text, the Pleiades record and the geography textbook. Still NOT verified: the dewclaw's position, how much plaster versus bare brick shows today, the exact outline of the north cliff from the terrace, and every colour (the palette and the rock colour are judgements). Check those against a photograph, or Bell's plates if found, before the painting is accepted. High confidence in the gate-6 verdict, two paws only with no head, masonry not rock, three claws per paw, the flat summit with no standing buildings, and the frescoes and mirror wall being on the west face and out of this view.
